title: What a fed quasi-star looks like
text:
This is the short companion to Quasi-stars under infall. That book records how the tools were built and tested: a steady envelope model, a Julia port of the radiation-hydrodynamics code TITAN, and continuum and non-LTE line transfer for its snapshots. This one keeps only what they predict for the spectrum of a quasi-star that is being fed, and asks how it compares with the Little Red Dots seen by JWST.
The object. A quasi-star of 10^6\,M_\odot (black hole of 10^5\,M_\odot inside), radius R = 8.4\times10^{15} cm, effective temperature 7300 K and luminosity 1.4\times10^{44} erg s^{-1} (Santarelli et al. 2026; Begelman and Dexter 2026). Gas falls onto it from 30R at 3\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}, freely, and stops in a radiative shock at the photosphere. TITAN follows the star and the infall through 4.5\times10^8 s (run W30).
What the spectrum shows, in one paragraph. The star’s own light keeps the infall ionized out to about 4R and partly ionized out to 100R. Its far ultraviolet does it through the Lyman lines, so the X-rays of the shock do not matter. Hα comes out in strong, narrow emission (equivalent width −800 Å, FWHM 360 km s^{-1}), with a steep Balmer decrement (5.1–5.3) and no dust anywhere. Hβ and the higher Balmer lines show deep redshifted absorption, the infall seen against the star. The Paschen and Brackett lines are strong, Lyα is weak, and the Balmer jump is 0.74 dex. The shock’s X-rays mostly do not escape: L_{2-10\,\rm keV}/L \approx 2\times10^{-4}. All of this is [computed] with the stated assumptions (Chapter 2).
The book in five chapters.

The full non-LTE calculation on the TITAN run (Chapter 2).
What LTE would have said, and why it is wrong here (Chapter 3).
A simple model that reproduces the full calculation with no transfer. Most of it is closed form, and it shows which ingredients matter (Chapter 4).
The whole emission spectrum, line by line and band by band, and what produces each part (Chapter 5).
The Little Red Dots: what JWST spectra show, and where this model agrees and where it does not (Chapter 6).







How to read the status of a statement



[computed]: output of the code in the repository, reproducible with the commands in Appendix A. [tested]: a computed result checked by a test or a deliberate variation. [estimate]: an order-of-magnitude argument. [interpretation]: our reading of the results, not separately derived. [observed]: a measurement reported in the literature, with its reference.

title: 2  The non-LTE spectrum of the TITAN quasi-star
text:
2.1 The model
The star. A 10^6\,M_\odot quasi-star with a 10^5\,M_\odot black hole, from the stellar-structure models of Santarelli et al. (2026): radius R = 8.4352\times10^{15} cm and luminosity L_0 = 1.420\times10^{44} erg s^{-1}. TITAN, ported to Julia, evolves its envelope in radiation hydrodynamics on an adaptive grid. It uses zero-metallicity LTE opacities, without lines, and mixing-length convection (details in the detailed book).
The infall. In run W30, gas enters through an outer boundary at 30R at 3\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1} and the free-fall speed. It reaches the star at v_{\rm ff}(R) = 1770 km s^{-1} and stops in a radiative shock at the photosphere. Behind the shock a thin cooling layer reaches 3.7\times10^7 K and radiates the kinetic power \tfrac12\dot M v^2 = 2.6\times10^{42} erg s^{-1}, 2 % of L_0, mostly as hard free–free emission. The star settles after a few dynamical times. From 2\times10^8 s to 4.5\times10^8 s its photosphere stays at r_{\rm ph} = 0.989R, T_{\rm eff} = 7310 \pm 17 K and L = 0.997\,L_0 [computed]. Moving the outer boundary from 1.2R to 30R changes none of this.
The spectrum calculation. It uses the snapshot at 4.18\times10^8 s.
The iteration took 140 passes. Over the last 40, without acceleration, the ionized fraction moved by at most 0.016 and n_2 by at most 3.7 % [computed].
crumbs: 2  The non-LTE spectrum of the TITAN quasi-star

title: 2  The non-LTE spectrum of the TITAN quasi-star
text:
Continuum: static spherical transfer through the star, the shock layer and the infall, out to 120R. Beyond TITAN’s 30R we assume the same free fall continues, with T \propto r^{-1/2}. It includes coherent Thomson scattering, and the temperatures below the shock are corrected to radiative equilibrium for the non-grey opacities (Unsöld–Lucy).
Hydrogen out of LTE: wherever the infall is cooler than 2\times10^4 K (118 points from just above the shock to 120R). The atom has twelve levels plus the proton. Collision rates are approximate, and line transfer uses Sobolev escape probabilities in the free-fall velocity field.
Coupling: the bound–free rates use the mean intensity from the full transfer, which in turn uses the non-LTE opacities and emissivities, iterated to convergence. X-rays above 100 eV make secondary ionizations.
Held fixed: TITAN’s temperatures and densities. Helium stays in LTE.

title: 2  The non-LTE spectrum of the TITAN quasi-star
section: 2.2 The infall is ionized by the star
text:
2.2 The infall is ionized by the star

Hydrogen is more than 99 % ionized out to 4.2R, 92 % at 8.5R, 50 % at 40R and 8 % at 120R [computed]. In LTE at the same temperatures it would be neutral beyond 2R (Chapter 3).

The neutral column is 8.5\times10^{23} cm^{-2} out of 9.0\times10^{24} cm^{-2} in all.
The infall has a Thomson depth of 5.4: an electron-scattering cocoon around the star.
The collision rates (×0.3, ×3), the X-rays (switched off) and the Lyman-continuum treatment were varied on the earlier run A220. None of them changes the neutral column by more than 10 % [tested].

What does ionize it is worked out in Chapter 4: the star’s far-UV light pumps the Lyman lines, and the excited atoms are photoionized by its optical light.

text:
2.3 Hα in strong emission
The Hα source function is above the local continuum everywhere in the infall (apart from a thin X-ray-heated layer just above the shock, below 0.9913R). S_L/J_c = 1.4 just above the star, 11 at 4.7R, 32 at 13R and about 60 at 30R. The line is optically thick: Sobolev depths range from 10 to 2800 [computed].

The profiles are integrated along rays through the infall with the non-LTE populations [computed].

Narrow. Most of the line forms far out, where the gas falls slowly. 79 % of the line power comes from beyond 5R, 51 % from beyond 12R and 17 % from beyond 30R [computed]. The free-fall speed is 560 km s^{-1} at 10R and 280 km s^{-1} at 40R.

Redshifted absorption in Hβ is the infall in front of the star, absorbing its light. Hα has none because its source function is above the continuum everywhere [interpretation].

title: 2  The non-LTE spectrum of the TITAN quasi-star
text:
2.4 Energy
The continuum carries 1.231\times10^{44} erg s^{-1}. The hydrogen lines carry 1.1\times10^{43} erg s^{-1} in the solution’s own line balance, or 1.65\times10^{43} erg s^{-1} summed over the 23 computed emergent profiles. The difference is discussed in Section 5.3. Together this is 0.92 of TITAN’s luminosity [computed]. The power in the lines is starlight, absorbed in the Balmer and Paschen continua and re-emitted. The accretion shock adds only 2 % of L.
The missing 8 % is absorbed by infall gas whose temperature is held fixed. In reality it would heat that gas, and the temperatures would have to be solved for together with the populations. That is the main approximation left in the calculation [interpretation].






TITAN’s infall or an assumed one



The same calculation on the earlier run A220 stopped TITAN’s grid at 1.2R and assumed the free fall beyond it. W30 replaces the assumption out to 30R with TITAN’s own infall. The gas there is up to 20 % warmer than assumed at 3–4 R, but every result above moves by no more than the iteration drift. The ionized fraction at 40R is 0.51 for A220 and 0.50 for W30, Hα has EW −795 and −805 Å, and the Balmer decrement is 5.07 and 5.28 [computed]. What is still assumed is the gas beyond 30R. It emits about 17 % of the line power and holds about two thirds of the neutral column.

title: 3  What LTE would have said
text:
3.1 Side by side
TITAN’s own opacities, and the first spectra computed from its snapshots, assume LTE: level populations and ionization set by the local temperature (Saha–Boltzmann). For the infall that assumption fails badly. Apart from a thin layer right above the shock, the gas is at 1000–6700 K, but it sees the radiation of a 7300 K star, diluted by geometry and enhanced in the far UV. Its hydrogen densities (6\times10^{8} cm^{-3} at the star down to 4\times10^{5} cm^{-3} at 120R) are far too low for collisions to enforce LTE.

title: 3  What LTE would have said
text:
3.2 What changes, and why

Ionization. In LTE the infall is neutral beyond 2R. Out of LTE it is ionized, because the excited levels are populated by the star’s radiation, not by the 1000–4000 K gas, and are then photoionized by its optical light (Chapter 4). This is the classic situation of a cool gas irradiated by a hot source, as in nebulae or stellar winds, where LTE is known to fail [interpretation].
Electron scattering. A Thomson depth of 5.4 instead of 0.6 means most of the star’s light is scattered several times on its way out. That traps the radiation (Chapter 4) and would broaden lines by electron scattering. Our line profiles leave this broadening out (Chapter 5).
Hα. LTE cannot decide even the sign of Hα: the result depends on the n=2 population and the source function, which LTE does not fix. The non-LTE source function is far above the thermal one in the outer infall, so the line is in emission and 40–80 times stronger than any LTE bracket.
Continuum. Photoionization from n=2 in the infall absorbs Balmer-continuum light. The Balmer jump deepens from 0.61 to 0.74 dex, and the optical band loses 14 %.
X-rays. The neutral column is ten times smaller, so a little more of the shock’s hard X-rays escape: 2–10 keV rises by 50 %. Below about 2 keV nothing escapes in either case, because helium, kept in LTE, is neutral.
crumbs: 3  What LTE would have said

title: 3  What LTE would have said
section: 3.3 The one thing LTE gets right
text:
3.3 The one thing LTE gets right
LTE does get the free-fall structure and the shock right, and with it the energy budget. The accretion shock radiates 2 % of L, the star does the rest, and T_{\rm eff} and L are TITAN’s. The emergent continuum shape changes, but only by redistributing that energy [computed].
crumbs: 3  What LTE would have said

title: 4  A simple model of the infall
text:
4.1 Structure in closed form
The full calculation needs a TITAN run, a spherical transfer code and 140 coupled iterations. This chapter builds a model that needs none of them, and tests each step against the full solution of Chapter 2. It has three levels:
Along the way it shows what actually sets the answer.
Steady free fall at \dot M onto a star of mass M and radius R:
v_{\rm ff} = \sqrt{2GM/r}, \qquad n_{\rm H}(r) = \frac{X\dot M}{4\pi r^2 v_{\rm ff}\,m_{\rm H}} = n_0\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^{-3/2},
\qquad N_{\rm H} = 2 n_0 R\left[1 - \sqrt{R/r_{\rm out}}\right].
For \dot M = 3\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}, M = 10^6\,M_\odot and R = 8.4\times10^{15} cm, this gives v_{\rm ff}(R) = 1770 km s^{-1}, n_0 = 5.4\times10^8 cm^{-3} and, out to 120R, N_{\rm H} = 8.3\times10^{24} cm^{-2} [computed]. TITAN’s infall follows this free fall to within 1–2 % beyond 1.2R (Chapter 2). Fully ionized, the column has Thomson depth \sigma_{\rm T}N_{\rm H} = 5.5. Half of the column (to 120R) lies within 3.4R of the star, because N_{\rm H}(<r) \propto 1 - (R/r)^{1/2}.
Radiation trapping. An electron-scattering envelope does not absorb the star’s light, but it makes the light random-walk. Then the mean intensity exceeds the geometrically diluted value W(r)I_\nu, with W = \tfrac12[1-\sqrt{1-(R/r)^2}]. In the Eddington approximation (K = J/3) for a sphere carrying the star’s flux:
J_\nu(r) = W(r)\,I_\nu + 3H_\nu(r)\,\tau^*(r), \qquad H_\nu = \frac{L_\nu}{16\pi^2 r^2}, \qquad
\tau^*(r) = r^2\int_r^\infty \frac{n_e\sigma_{\rm T}}{r'^2}\,dr' .
For n_e \propto r^{-3/2}, \tau^* = \tau_{\rm es}/5, so near the star J/J_{\rm geom} \approx 1 + 0.3\,\tau_{\rm es}
\approx 2.5. In the full solution, J(\mathrm{H}\alpha)/[W B_\nu(T_{\rm eff})] is 2.0–2.5 within 2R and falls to 1.2 at 20R [computed]. A plane-parallel estimate, 1 + 1.5\,\tau_{\rm es} \approx 9, would be four times too large.
crumbs: 4  A simple model of the infall

title: 4  A simple model of the infall
text:
4.2 What ionizes the infall
The full solution answers this directly (julia/nlte_rates.jl) [computed]:

The Lyman continuum is in detailed balance. About half of all photoionizations are from the ground state, but they are balanced by recombinations to it, to 10^{-4} of all recombinations beyond 1.2R. The Lyman-continuum radiation is the infall’s own recombination light, reabsorbed nearby. That is case B, as in a nebula.
The net ionization comes from n = 2. Photoionization from n=2 by Balmer-continuum light exceeds recombination to n=2 by 0.10–0.35 of all recombinations, increasing outwards. This balances the recombinations to n \ge 4 that cascade down. From n=3 the net rate is small and changes sign.
What keeps n=2 populated is far-UV light. At 1000 Å the mean intensity in the infall is 400–1200 times that of a 7310 K blackbody, diluted.

The decisive test replaces bands of the full solution’s own J_\nu with the diluted, trapped light of a 7310 K blackbody, and recomputes the populations at fixed temperatures [computed]:

Only the far UV matters. It contains Lyα (1216 Å) and Lyβ (1026 Å): continuum light at those wavelengths pumps the optically thick Lyman lines. That fills n = 2 and n = 3, and the star’s ordinary optical light ionizes them.
Where the far UV comes from. The answer is the star itself, not the shock. The emergent spectrum of the TITAN star without any infall (star_t0) is 772 times a 7310 K blackbody at 1000 Å, 78 times at Lyα and 13 times at 1500 Å. Above the Balmer edge it is within a factor 1.2 of the blackbody [computed]. Between the Lyman and Balmer edges, a zero-metallicity photosphere without line opacity has a window: there we see deep, hot layers. With the star’s spectrum in place of the blackbody in that band, the full-J test returns a neutral column of 5.7\times10^{23} cm^{-2} [computed].






The weak point



The infall’s ionization, and with it the Hα, rests on the star’s far-UV excess. That excess comes from a photosphere computed in LTE, with continuum opacities only. The Lyman lines, Lyα above all, would absorb part of it, and metals would absorb more. Below, the far UV is reduced by up to a factor 1000 to see how much this matters.

title: 4  A simple model of the infall
section: 4.3 A closed formula for the ionization
text:
4.3 A closed formula for the ionization
Take the three findings as assumptions:

the Lyman continuum is in detailed balance (case B);
Lyα and Lyβ are thick and in radiative balance with the star’s far UV, so n_2/n_1 = (g_2/g_1)\,J_{\rm Ly\alpha}/(2h\nu^3/c^2) and the same for n_3 with Lyβ;
n=2 and n=3 are photoionized by the Balmer and Paschen continua.

Both the pumping and the ionizing light scale with the same dilution-and-trapping factor f(r) = W + 3\tau^* R^2/4r^2. Ionization balance per volume, with n_e = n_p = x\,n_{\rm H}, then gives

\frac{x^2}{1-x} = \frac{f(r)^2\,Q_0}{n_{\rm H}(r)\,\alpha_B(T)}, \qquad
Q_0 = \frac{g_2 I_{\rm Ly\alpha}}{g_1\,2h\nu_{\alpha}^3/c^2}\,\Gamma_2 + \frac{g_3 I_{\rm Ly\beta}}{g_1\,2h\nu_{\beta}^3/c^2}\,\Gamma_3 ,

with \Gamma_i = 4\pi\int I_\nu\sigma_i\,d\nu/h\nu the undiluted photoionization rates, all from the star’s spectrum. For the TITAN star: (g_2/g_1)I_{\rm Ly\alpha}/(2h\nu^3/c^2) = 2.7\times10^{-5}, \Gamma_2 = 1.6\times10^5 s^{-1} and \Gamma_3 = 8.0\times10^5 s^{-1}. The only other input is \alpha_B(T) (julia/closed_form.jl).
Far out, f \approx (R/2r)^2 and n_{\rm H} \propto r^{-3/2}, so the right-hand side falls as r^{-5/2}. The infall is fully ionized where it exceeds 1, and beyond, the ionized fraction falls roughly as x \propto r^{-5/4} (a little faster, since \alpha_B grows as the gas cools).

title: 4  A simple model of the infall
text:
4.5 Hα in closed form
In an optically thick Sobolev line the power escaping per unit volume is (4\pi\nu_0/c)(S_L - J)\langle Q\rangle, with \langle Q\rangle the angle-averaged velocity gradient. For free fall, \langle Q\rangle = (v/r)\langle|1-\tfrac32\mu^2|\rangle = 0.589\,v/r. Hence

L_{\rm line} = \frac{16\pi^2\nu_0}{c}\;0.589\int r\,v_{\rm ff}(r)\,\bigl[S_L(r) - J_\nu(r)\bigr]\,dr .

With the full solution’s S_L and J, this gives L({\rm H\alpha}) = 1.08\times10^{43} erg s^{-1}, against 1.10\times10^{43} from the exact Sobolev rates [computed]. Hα is thick everywhere it matters.
The source function falls roughly as S_L \propto r^{-1.2} out to 20R: 0.95\,B_\nu(T_{\rm eff}) at 1.2R and 0.034\,B_\nu at 20R. Beyond that it falls faster. With v_{\rm ff} \propto r^{-1/2}, the integrand goes as r^{-0.7}, so L({\rm H\alpha}) \propto r_{\rm out}^{0.3}. A factor 10 in the outer radius is a factor 2 in Hα. This is what the earlier extension test found: ending the infall at 12R instead of 120R halved the lines.
crumbs: 4  A simple model of the infall

title: 4  A simple model of the infall
text:
4.6 What the simple model says

The infall is a Thomson-thick, partly ionized cocoon: N_{\rm H} = 2n_0R, \tau_{\rm es} \approx 5 [computed].
It is ionized by the star’s own light, in two steps. The far UV pumps the Lyman lines, and the optical continuum photoionizes the excited atoms. The Lyman continuum is in case-B balance, and the shock’s X-rays do not matter [computed].
A one-line formula reproduces the ionized fraction to about 0.2 and the neutral column to 10 % [computed].
Hα is thick everywhere it matters. Its luminosity is an integral of r\,v\,S_L and grows slowly with the extent of the infall, as r_{\rm out}^{0.3} [computed].
The weak point is the star’s far UV, which no calculation here has done with lines [interpretation].
crumbs: 4  A simple model of the infall

title: 5  The full emission spectrum
text:
5.1 The continuum
The figure shows the emergent spectrum of the non-LTE solution: the continuum, with 23 hydrogen lines computed one by one and multiplied onto it. For comparison, the TITAN star before any infall is shown (continuum only). From the far UV to the near infrared, each feature has a definite origin.
The photosphere (T_{\rm eff} = 7310 K) makes almost all of the light. Above the Balmer edge its spectrum is within a factor 1.2 of a blackbody at T_{\rm eff}. Below the edge it has a far-UV excess: 13 times the blackbody at 1500 Å, 78 times at Lyα, 770 times at 1000 Å. Between the Lyman and Balmer edges a zero-metallicity photosphere has little continuum opacity, so the light there comes from deeper, hotter layers. Our opacities contain no lines, so this excess is probably overestimated [computed; interpretation]. It powers the ionization of the infall (Chapter 4).
The Balmer jump grows from 0.23 dex for the bare star to 0.74 dex. The infall absorbs Balmer-continuum light in photoionizations from n = 2, the very process that keeps it ionized. In LTE, with neutral, Boltzmann-populated gas, the jump is 0.61 dex [computed]. A strong Balmer break here is a sign of dense gas around the star with a populated n=2, not of an old stellar population [interpretation].
Electron scattering. The Thomson depth of 5.4 does not change the continuum’s shape, because the scattering is coherent and grey. It traps the light (Chapter 4) and lengthens the photons’ path, which strengthens every absorption in the infall.
X-rays. The shock heats the post-shock gas to 3.7\times10^7 K, and \tfrac12\dot M v^2 = 2.6\times10^{42} erg s^{-1} is radiated as free–free emission, 7.3\times10^{41} erg s^{-1} of it above 2 keV. Only 4.7\times10^{40} erg s^{-1} escapes above 2 keV, through a column of 9\times10^{24} cm^{-2} that is Thomson-thick and partly neutral. Nothing escapes below about 2 keV [computed]. Helium, held in LTE and therefore neutral, sets that cut-off. If the star’s far UV ionized helium as well, it could move. That is not computed. The ratio L_{2-10\,\rm keV}/L \approx 2\times10^{-4} makes this an X-ray-weak source.

Why Hα is so strong. In the outer infall the populations of n=2 and n=3 are set by the star’s far UV, not by the cold gas. The Hα source function there is 10–60 times the local continuum. The line is optically thick everywhere (Sobolev depth 10–2800), so its luminosity is the thick-line integral \propto\int r\,v\,S_L\,dr (Section 4.5). The line luminosity is starlight, absorbed in the Balmer and Paschen continua and re-emitted. It is not recombination radiation powered by the accretion. The shock’s X-rays could drive at most a few 10^{40} erg s^{-1} of Hα through the ionizations they make [estimate].
Why it is narrow. Half of the power comes from beyond 12R, where the gas falls at less than about 500 km s^{-1}. The FWHM is 360 km s^{-1}. The wings reach −1100 and +1700 km s^{-1}: the red wing comes from the gas falling onto the near side of the star at up to 1770 km s^{-1} [computed; interpretation]. Our profiles leave out electron scattering in the line, and with \tau_{\rm es} \approx 5 that would broaden the wings. That is the most important omission for comparing profiles with observations (Chapter 6).
The Balmer decrement, L({\rm H\alpha})/L({\rm H\beta}) = 5.3 (case B: 2.86), owes nothing to dust. Both lines are optically thick, and each line’s luminosity is set by its source function and the velocity field, not by recombination statistics. Hβ is further weakened by absorption against the star: it has a trough down to 3 % of the continuum at +160 km s^{-1}. The decrement depends on how the line power is counted. From the solution’s own local line powers it would be 8.9 instead of 5.3 (Section 5.3). Either way it is far from case B [computed].
Redshifted Balmer absorption. From Hβ upwards every Balmer line has an absorption trough at +160 to +180 km s^{-1}, down to 3–8 % of the continuum, and from Hε up absorption wins over emission. The gas between us and the star falls away from us, so its absorption is redshifted. Its source function in these lines is below the stellar intensity behind it. Redshifted absorption is the kinematic signature of infall [computed; interpretation].
Paschen and Brackett lines are strong: together 5.2\times10^{42} erg s^{-1}, 57 % of Hα. Their equivalent widths are huge, Paα −3200 Å and Brα −7000 Å, because the stellar continuum is faint in the infrared. Paα/Hα = 0.19 [computed].
Lyα is weak: 0.054 of Hα, against about 10 in case B for nebulae. Lyα is so optically thick that its photons scatter until they are destroyed, mostly when the excited atom is photoionized from n=2. The higher Lyman lines are in net absorption [computed; interpretation].

title: 5  The full emission spectrum
text:
5.3 The energy in the lines
The 23 emergent profiles carry 1.65\times10^{43} erg s^{-1}. The solution’s own net line power (Sobolev escape, summed over all 66 transitions of the model atom) is 1.12\times10^{43} erg s^{-1}. Line by line (julia/nlte_linepower.jl) [computed]:

For the strong emission lines, the emergent luminosity is 0.8–1.4 times the local net power: Hα 0.81, Lyα 0.81, Paα 0.87, Paβ to Brδ 0.94–1.32, Hβ 1.37.
Most of the difference is in Hγ–Hθ. In the local balance they absorb 5.1\times10^{42} erg s^{-1} of continuum. In the emergent spectrum they are close to neutral, +0.2\times10^{42}.
The local balance counts all the light the gas absorbs, including light headed inwards to the star. The emergent profile counts only what is removed from the light that leaves. With temperatures held fixed, energy absorbed from the inward light goes nowhere, so the two need not agree [interpretation].

So the strong lines are uncertain by 20–40 %, and the total line luminosity by about 50 %.

title: 5  The full emission spectrum
section: 5.4 What is not in this spectrum
text:
5.4 What is not in this spectrum

Electron-scattering wings of the lines, expected with \tau_{\rm es} \approx 5.
Helium lines and non-LTE helium. The soft X-ray cut-off depends on it.
Metals: none, since the model is at zero metallicity. So there is no Fe II, O I, Na D or Ca II.
Thermal balance of the infall. It absorbs 8 % of L at fixed temperature.
The infall beyond 30R, which is assumed out to 120R.
Line opacity in the star’s own photosphere, which would reduce the far-UV excess (Chapter 4).
Asphericity. Everything here is spherical: one viewing angle, no disc, no outflow.
